Teaching R, data visualisation and text mining: my Big Data course, Fall 2023

In the fall of 2023 I taught a Big Data & Data Visualisation course at the MNB Institute of John von Neumann University. The idea was to help students analyse, understand and communicate about their data, with R as the tool. Classes met on Tuesday afternoons in a computer lab.

Why this course

Data analysis and visualisation have become some of the most important skills in business and, above all, in research. But handling data properly is not trivial. The course introduced statistical and visualisation methods, such as advanced inferential statistics and dimension reduction, and put a lot of effort into helping students use a programming language properly, so they could apply these tools in practice.

The plan

The semester was planned as eleven weeks, from the first steps in R to text mining. It was a plan, not a promise: the agenda could change as we learned how much prior knowledge the students had.

  1. Introduction to R, descriptive statistics
  2. Data manipulation I
  3. Data manipulation II, functional programming
  4. Regression, classification
  5. Data visualisation I
  6. Data visualisation II, tools for publishing
  7. Causality
  8. Tidy modelling
  9. Clustering
  10. Web scraping, dimension reduction
  11. Text mining

Free reading

The course focuses on the technical side of data analysis, which evolves quickly, so the readings are free and mostly available online. The books I recommended most were R for Data Science (Wickham, Çetinkaya-Rundel and Grolemund), An Introduction to Statistical Learning with Applications in R, Tidy Modeling with R (Kuhn and Silge) and ggplot2: Elegant Graphics for Data Analysis. For a broader view I added Data Analysis for Business, Economics, and Policy by Gábor Békés and Gábor Kézdi, and Storytelling with Data by Cole Nussbaumer Knaflic.

Assignments in R

Assignments ran as interactive learnr tutorials in R, so students practised in the same language they used in class.

Open materials

The syllabus, the schedule with readings and slides, and the assignments are all on the course site. The content is licensed under Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial 4.0 (CC BY-NC 4.0), so you are welcome to use it for learning and teaching.
